questions.q: In the Bellman-Ford equation Dx(y) = min_v { c(x,v) + Dv(y) }, the minimum is taken over which set of nodes v?
choices: All neighbors v of x
All nodes v in the network
All nodes on the current path from x to y
All neighbors v of the destination y
questions.explain: x tries each of its own neighbors as the first hop and adds the direct link cost c(x,v) to that neighbor's estimate Dv(y). Because the minimum only covers neighbors, a DV node needs information from its neighbors and nothing else.

questions.q: In Dx(y) = min_v { c(x,v) + Dv(y) }, what does the term Dv(y) stand for?
choices: Neighbor v's estimated least-cost-path cost to y
The direct cost of the link from v to y
The direct cost of the link from x to v
The number of hops from v to y
questions.explain: c(x,v) is the direct cost of the link from x to v. Dv(y) is v's own estimate of its least-cost path to y, which v reports in its distance vector.

questions.q: Node u has neighbors v, x and w with link costs c(u,v) = 2, c(u,x) = 1, c(u,w) = 5. For destination z, the neighbors report Dv(z) = 5, Dx(z) = 3, Dw(z) = 3. Using Bellman-Ford, what is Du(z)?
Node u has neighbors v, x and w with c(u,v) = 2, c(u,x) = 1, c(u,w) = 5, and they report Dv(z) = 5, Dx(z) = 3, Dw(z) = 3. Which node is u's next hop toward z?
choices: v
x
w
z itself
questions.explain: The next hop is the neighbor that achieves the minimum in the Bellman-Ford equation. Here that is x, with 1 + 3 = 4. w also reports a distance of 3, but its link from u costs 5, so going through w costs 8.

questions.q: Node u has neighbors v, x and w. They report Dv(z) = 5, Dx(z) = 3, Dw(z) = 3, and c(u,v) = 2, c(u,w) = 5. The link u–x now costs 6, and the neighbors' reported values are unchanged. What is Du(z)?
questions.explain: min{2+5, 6+3, 5+3} = min{7, 9, 8} = 7. The minimum is now reached through v, so v becomes u's next hop toward z.

questions.q: The Bellman-Ford equation that distance-vector routing is based on is an example of which technique?
choices: Dynamic programming
Greedy selection of the closest not-yet-finalized node
Divide and conquer
Random flooding
questions.explain: Bellman-Ford is dynamic programming. It writes x's least cost to y in terms of the least costs of x's neighbors to y, which are solutions to smaller subproblems.

questions.q: To compute Dx(y) with the Bellman-Ford equation, node x must know the complete network topology.
questions.explain: x only needs the costs of its own links, c(x,v), and the distance vectors Dv(y) that its neighbors report. It never needs the full topology.

questions.q: In the distance-vector algorithm, what can cause a node to start a local iteration (recompute its DV)?
choices: A change in the cost of one of its local links
A DV update message from a neighbor
A command from a central controller
A link-state broadcast from every router in the network
questions.explain: DV is iterative and asynchronous. A local iteration is triggered only by a change in a local link cost or a DV update message from a neighbor. No central controller is involved, and routers do not flood the network.

questions.q: Which sequence matches the loop each DV node runs?
choices: Wait for a local link cost change or a neighbor's message → recompute DV estimates → if the DV to any destination changed, notify neighbors
Recompute DV estimates → notify all neighbors → wait for acknowledgments from every router
Wait for a neighbor's message → notify neighbors → recompute DV estimates
Flood local link costs to all routers → build the full topology → compute least-cost paths
questions.explain: Each node repeats three steps: wait for an event (a local link cost change or a message from a neighbor), recompute its DV estimates using the DVs it received, and notify its neighbors only if its DV to some destination changed.

questions.q: After a DV node recomputes its distance vector, when does it send the new DV to its neighbors?
choices: Only if its DV to some destination changed
Every time it recomputes, whether or not anything changed
Only when a neighbor explicitly asks for it
Never; neighbors read it directly from the node's table
questions.explain: DV is distributed and self-stopping. A node notifies its neighbors only when its DV changes, and those neighbors pass the change on only if their own DVs change.

questions.q: DV is called self-stopping: once DVs stop changing, no notifications are sent, and a node that receives no notification takes no action.
questions.explain: When no node's DV changes, no one sends a notification. With nothing received, no node recomputes, so the algorithm stops on its own.

questions.q: Under minor, natural conditions, each DV estimate Dx(y) converges to the actual least cost dx(y).
questions.explain: Nodes repeatedly exchange DVs and apply Bellman-Ford. Under minor, natural conditions, the estimates Dx(y) converge to the true least costs dx(y).

questions.q: When node x receives a new distance vector from a neighbor, which of its own estimates does it update with the Bellman-Ford equation?
choices: Dx(y) for every destination y in the network
Only Dx(v), its distance to the neighbor v that sent the DV
Only the link cost c(x,v) to that neighbor
None; it just forwards the received DV to its other neighbors
questions.explain: x recomputes Dx(y) ← min_v { c(x,v) + Dv(y) } for each node y in N. Link costs are measured locally and are not taken from neighbors' DVs.

questions.q: In the distance-vector example, what does each node's distance vector contain at t = 0?
choices: Costs to its direct neighbors (and 0 to itself); every other entry is ∞
Least costs to every node in the network
Costs to every node within two hops
∞ for every entry, including itself
questions.explain: At t = 0, each node only has distance estimates to its nearest neighbors, which are the link costs, plus 0 to itself. Every other destination is ∞. Each node then sends this local DV to its neighbors.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. At t = 0, each node knows only the costs of its own links. At each later step, every node receives its neighbors' DVs from the previous step, recomputes, and sends. At t = 1, b receives the t = 0 DVs of a, c and e. What is b's new Db(d)?
questions.explain: Db(d) = min{ c(b,a)+Da(d), c(b,c)+Dc(d), c(b,e)+De(d) } = min{8+1, 1+∞, 1+1} = 2, through e.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. At t = 0, each node knows only the costs of its own links. At t = 1, b receives the t = 0 DVs of a, c and e. What does b compute for Db(g)?
questions.explain: None of b's neighbors (a, c, e) is adjacent to g, so all of them had Dx(g) = ∞ at t = 0. Every term in the minimum is ∞, which means information about g hasn't reached b yet. The other entries b computes at t = 1 are a = 8, c = 1, d = 2, e = 1, f = 2, h = 2, i = ∞.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. At t = 1, c receives b's t = 0 DV (Db(a) = 8, Db(b) = 0, Db(c) = 1, Db(e) = 1, all others ∞). What is c's new Dc(a)?
questions.explain: c's only neighbor is b, so Dc(a) = c(c,b) + Db(a) = 1 + 8 = 9. c doesn't know about the cheaper route c–b–e–d–a (cost 4) yet. That information arrives over later iterations.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. After c recomputes at t = 1 using b's t = 0 DV, which of these entries in c's DV are finite?
choices: Dc(a)
Dc(d)
Dc(e)
Dc(f)
Dc(h)
questions.explain: Dc(a) = 1 + 8 = 9 and Dc(e) = 1 + 1 = 2. b's t = 0 DV had ∞ for d, f and h, so those entries stay ∞. f is drawn right below c, but there is no c–f link.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. At t = 1, e receives the t = 0 DVs of its neighbors b, d, f and h. What is e's new De(a)?
questions.explain: Through b: 1 + Db(a) = 1 + 8 = 9. Through d: 1 + Dd(a) = 1 + 1 = 2. Through f and h: ∞. So De(a) = 2, with d as the next hop.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. At t = 1, e receives the t = 0 DVs of b, d, f and h. What is e's new DV?
questions.explain: Each neighbor link costs 1, so e adds 1 to the best neighbor report for each destination: a through d (1+1), c through b (1+1), g through d or h (1+1), and i through f or h (1+1). Its own neighbors b, d, f, h stay at 1, and e stays at 0.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Link a–b costs 8. Links b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i each cost 1. There is no c–f link. a starts with Da(b) = 8, the direct link. At each step, every node receives its neighbors' DVs from the previous step, recomputes, and sends. When a recomputes at t = 2, what is Da(b)?
questions.explain: At t = 1, d computes Dd(b) = min{1+8 via a, 1+1 via e, ∞ via g} = 2. At t = 2, a receives that value: Da(b) = min{8 + Db(b), 1 + Dd(b)} = min{8+0, 1+2} = 3. a's next hop to b switches from the expensive direct link to d.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Links: a–b, b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i (no c–f link). DV runs in synchronous steps starting at t = 0. At what time step t can c's state from t = 0 first influence DV computations at node e?
questions.explain: Information moves one hop per communicate-and-compute step. e is 2 hops from c (c–b–e), so c's t = 0 state can affect e's computation at t = 2.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Links: a–b, b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i (no c–f link). DV runs in synchronous steps starting at t = 0. At what time step t can c's state from t = 0 first influence DV computations at node i?
questions.explain: i is 4 hops from c, for example c–b–e–f–i or c–b–e–h–i. c's state reaches b at t = 1, a and e at t = 2, d, f and h at t = 3, and g and i at t = 4.

questions.q: Grid network: top row a, b, c; middle row d, e, f; bottom row g, h, i. Links: a–b, b–c, a–d, b–e, d–e, e–f, d–g, e–h, f–i, g–h, h–i (no c–f link). DV runs in synchronous steps starting at t = 0. Which nodes are first reached by c's t = 0 state at t = 3?
choices: a
d
f
g
h
i
questions.explain: d, f and h are exactly 3 hops from c (through b and then e). a is 2 hops away (t = 2). g and i are 4 hops away (t = 4).

questions.q: In the grid example (top row a, b, c; middle d, e, f; bottom g, h, i), why doesn't c's t = 0 state influence f until t = 3, even though f is drawn directly below c?
choices: There is no c–f link, so f is 3 hops from c (c–b–e–f)
The c–f link has a large cost, so updates over it are delayed
f only accepts updates every third step
f receives c's DV at t = 1 but ignores it until t = 3
questions.explain: The c–f link is missing, which is one of the example's deliberate asymmetries. DV information spreads one hop per step, and the shortest hop path from c to f is c–b–e–f.

questions.q: In the grid example (a–b costs 8; all other links cost 1), c's t = 0 state reaches d before it reaches a, because the high cost of the a–b link slows the spread toward a.
questions.explain: Diffusion is counted in hops (one hop per iteration), not link cost. a is 2 hops from c and is reached at t = 2. d is 3 hops away and is reached at t = 3.

questions.q: In general, after t rounds of DV communication and computation, a node's state from t = 0 can have influenced DV computations at nodes up to how far away?
choices: t hops
2t hops
A total path cost of t
The whole network, from t = 1 on
questions.explain: Each round of communication and computation pushes the state one hop further, so after t rounds it can influence nodes up to t hops away.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y costs 4, y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50, and DV has converged. What is z's least cost to x, Dz(x)?
questions.explain: Dz(x) = min{ c(z,x) + 0, c(z,y) + Dy(x) } = min{50, 1+4} = 5, through y.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y costs 4, y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50, and DV has converged. The x–y link cost drops to 1. y detects the change, updates its DV and informs its neighbors, and then z recomputes. What is z's new Dz(x)?
questions.explain: y's new Dy(x) is 1. z computes min{50, 1 + 1} = 2 and sends its new DV to its neighbors.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y costs 4, y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50. The x–y cost drops to 1, y updates and informs z, and z updates and sends its DV. When y receives z's update, y's least costs don't change, so y does not send z another message.
questions.explain: y still reaches x for 1 over the direct link, so its DV is unchanged and it stays quiet. The update is complete after just a couple of steps, which is why good news travels fast.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y costs 4, y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50, and DV has converged, so z has reported Dz(x) = 5. The x–y link cost rises to 60. y detects the change and recomputes. What does y compute for its new Dy(x)?
questions.explain: Dy(x) = min{ c(y,x), c(y,z) + Dz(x) } = min{60, 1 + 5} = 6, through z. y then tells z its new cost to x is 6.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y costs 4, y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50. The x–y link rises to 60, and y computes a new cost of 6 to x through z because z had reported Dz(x) = 5. Why is y's estimate wrong?
choices: z's reported cost of 5 was a path through y itself over the old 4-cost link, so y is relying on stale information about a path through itself
y should always prefer a direct link over any path through a neighbor
z's cost of 5 was wrong even before the change; z's true cost had been 50 all along
The Bellman-Ford equation doesn't apply once a link cost increases
questions.explain: z's cost of 5 was z → y → x using the old x–y cost of 4. That path no longer costs 5, but y can't tell, because a DV only reports costs and not the paths behind them. This is what starts count-to-infinity.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y costs 4, y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50. After the x–y link rises to 60, y computes Dy(x) = 6 (through z) and notifies z. What does z compute for its new Dz(x)?
questions.explain: z's path to x goes through y, so z computes min{50, 1 + 6} = 7 and tells y. y then computes 8, z computes 9, and so on. The costs climb a little at a time, which is count-to-infinity.

questions.q: Three routers: x, y, z. While y believes its best path to x is through z, and z believes its best path to x is through y, what happens to a packet at y that is destined for x?
choices: It bounces back and forth between y and z in a routing loop
It is delivered over the direct x–y link
It is delivered over the direct x–z link
It is dropped immediately because y's cost to x is ∞
questions.explain: y forwards the packet to z, and z forwards it back to y. Routing loops like this are one of the DV problems listed in the comparison with LS.

questions.q: Three routers: link x–y now costs 60 (raised from 4), y–z costs 1, x–z costs 50. Once count-to-infinity ends and the network has converged, what is y's least cost to x, Dy(x)?
questions.explain: z's best route to x is now its direct link (50), because going through y would cost at least 61. y's best route is through z: min{60, 1 + 50} = 51.

questions.q: In distance-vector routing, what do the phrases "good news travels fast" and "bad news travels slow" refer to?
choices: A link cost decrease spreads in a few iterations, while a cost increase can trigger the slow count-to-infinity problem
Link-state messages travel faster than DV messages
Routers send cost decreases with higher priority than cost increases
Routers ignore cost increases until a timeout expires
questions.explain: When the x–y cost dropped from 4 to 1, the update finished in a couple of steps. When it rose from 4 to 60, y and z kept raising their costs one step at a time, because each relied on the other's outdated path.

questions.q: After a link cost increases, two DV routers can keep raising their costs to a destination in small steps, because each believes the other has a path to it. What is this problem called?
questions.explain: Count-to-infinity, also called bad news travels slow. Distributed algorithms are tricky!

questions.q: How do LS and DV compare in message complexity?
choices: LS: with n routers, O(n²) messages sent; DV: messages are exchanged only between neighbors, and convergence time varies
LS: messages are exchanged only between neighbors; DV: O(n²) messages sent
Both send O(n) messages
LS: O(n) messages; DV: O(n³) messages
questions.explain: In LS, every router's link costs must reach all n routers, which takes O(n²) messages. In DV, a router only exchanges messages with its neighbors, and how long it takes to converge varies.

questions.q: Which convergence issues belong to DV rather than LS?
choices: May have routing loops
Count-to-infinity problem
Convergence time varies
May have oscillations
O(n²) algorithm
questions.explain: DV: convergence time varies, it may have routing loops, and it has the count-to-infinity problem. LS: an O(n²) algorithm with O(n²) messages, and it may have oscillations.

questions.q: A malfunctioning or compromised DV router advertises that it has a really low-cost path to everywhere, so traffic gets pulled toward it. What is this called?
questions.explain: Black-holing. A DV router can advertise an incorrect path cost, and since other routers build their DVs from it, the bad cost draws traffic toward that router.

questions.q: In terms of robustness, what incorrect information can a malfunctioning router advertise under LS, compared with DV?
choices: LS: an incorrect link cost; DV: an incorrect path cost
LS: an incorrect path cost; DV: an incorrect link cost
Both: only an incorrect hop count
LS: nothing at all; DV: an incorrect link cost
questions.explain: An LS router advertises costs of its own links, so a bad LS router can misreport a link cost. A DV router advertises path costs to destinations, so a bad DV router can misreport a path cost, which can lead to black-holing.

questions.q: Why does a malfunctioning router's error stay more contained under LS than under DV?
choices: In LS each router computes only its own table, while in DV each router's DV is used by others, so errors propagate through the network
LS routers cannot advertise incorrect information
DV routers compute their tables only once, so errors are never corrected
LS messages are encrypted, so they can't be faked
questions.explain: Under LS, every router computes its own table, so a bad link cost doesn't arrive already mixed into other routers' results. Under DV, every router's DV is built from its neighbors' DVs, so one bad DV spreads through the network.

questions.q: In DV, a router that advertises a wrong path cost affects only its own forwarding decisions.
questions.explain: Each router's DV is used by its neighbors in their Bellman-Ford computations, and their DVs are then used by their neighbors. The error spreads through the network.
